name: Wildroot Cream-Oil

lead: Wildroot Cream-Oil was a men's hair-grooming product of the 1940s to 1960s from the Wildroot company of Buffalo, New York. Its main ingredient was lanolin, which conditions the hair and gives light hold for a tidy look.
It was heavily advertised on radio and television and is linked in popular memory to 1950s hair styling. It is now a vintage product, and a Wildroot Hair Groom is still sold by another company.

paras: A small amount was worked through the hair to condition and set the style. The Finger Nail Test in print advertising urged men to check for dryness and loose dandruff.
Lanolin can cause skin irritation or allergy in some people. Wildroot drew a Federal Trade Commission rebuke in 1937 over its health and results claims.

lead: Wildroot Cream-Oil was a hair tonic sold in the United States from the 1940s to the 1960s by the Wildroot company of Buffalo, New York [1]. It was an alcohol-free formula whose main ingredient was lanolin, and was used to condition hair and keep it neatly styled [1].

The product debuted in 1943 after wartime alcohol shortages pushed chemist Emanuel Gundlach to develop an alcohol-free alternative to the company's original tonic [1]. It was later associated with the slicked hair of 1950s teenage "greasers" [1].

paras: Wildroot sold hair tonic from 1911, aimed mainly at women in the 1920s and then at men from the 1930s; the Federal Trade Commission criticised its health and result claims in 1937 [1]. Gundlach's alcohol-free formula was initially planned as a tube-packaged cream, which executives rejected, so the company bottled a more watery version that sold well [1].

Advertising used a catchy radio jingle and print ads featuring the Finger Nail Test. Wildroot sponsored radio shows including The Adventures of Sam Spade (1946-50), Charlie Wild, Private Detective (1950-51), The Shadow and the King Cole Trio, and TV shows including The Adventures of Robin Hood and Perry Mason; cartoonist Al Capp's detective Fearless Fosdick endorsed it in the 1950s [1]. Colgate-Palmolive bought the company in 1959 for $10.5 million [1].

The product is described as emulsion containing lanolin, mineral oil and waxes, with a light, non-greasy finish compared with oily pomades [2]. These details come from an AI-generated encyclopedia and are less reliable than the history above.
